item.title: Glenohumeral Posterior Glide
clinicalUse: Limited flexion/internal rotation when posterior glide is relevant
patientPosition: Arm positioned comfortably near resting position initially.
therapistPosition: Support the arm and stay close to the joint line.
stabilization: Stabilize the scapula/acromial region so the humeral head glide is isolated.
contact: One hand supports the proximal humerus; the mobilizing hand contacts the anterior humeral head/proximal humerus broadly.
forceDirection: Posterior glide of the humeral head relative to the glenoid.
Low grade in pain-dominant stage; higher grade when stiffness dominates and irritability is low.
steps: 1. Record shoulder ROM and painful arc.
4. Progress only if pain remains acceptable.
6. Add active reaching and rotator-cuff/scapular exercise.
mistakes: Letting scapula move instead of humeral head.
Using aggressive Grade IV in highly irritable adhesive capsulitis.
Pushing directly into anterior shoulder pain.
safety: Avoid in acute dislocation, fracture, unstable postoperative restrictions or severe acute inflammatory states.
item.visualCue: Scapula fixed → Humeral head glides posteriorly → Re-test flexion/IR.

subTechniques.name: Glenohumeral Posterior Glide
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Improve a painful/restricted flexion or internal-rotation comparable sign when a posterior glide produces a useful response.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine with the scapula supported and the shoulder near a comfortable resting position; progress arm position only as irritability allows.
subTechniques.contact: Stabilize the scapula/acromial region. Use a broad contact over the anterior proximal humerus close to the joint line.
subTechniques.direction: Apply a posterior translation of the humeral head. Use Grade I–II for pain-dominant presentations and Grade III–IV only when stiffness dominates and irritability is low.
subTechniques.dosage: 30–60 seconds of oscillation for 2–4 bouts, with immediate re-test after each bout.
subTechniques.reassess: Shoulder flexion, internal rotation, painful arc and functional reach.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: If the scapula moves with the humerus, you are no longer isolating a glenohumeral glide.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid in acute dislocation, fracture or unstable postoperative states.

subTechniques.name: Glenohumeral Inferior Glide
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Improve elevation/abduction when inferior joint play is clinically relevant.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine with the arm supported in a comfortable amount of abduction.
subTechniques.contact: Stabilize the scapula. Contact the proximal humerus close to the joint line with a broad comfortable grip.
subTechniques.direction: Direct the humeral head inferiorly relative to the glenoid using the selected Maitland grade.
subTechniques.dosage: 30–60 seconds × 2–4 bouts, reassessing elevation after each set.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Do not pull from the distal arm; keep the force close to the joint so the glide is controlled.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Respect inferior instability and postoperative precautions.

subTechniques.name: Glenohumeral Anterior Glide
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Selected trial for extension/external-rotation restriction when an anterior glide improves the comparable sign.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Prone or supine in a position that permits safe stabilization without stressing the anterior capsule.
subTechniques.contact: Stabilize the scapula; contact the posterior proximal humerus broadly.
subTechniques.direction: Apply a controlled anterior glide. Begin with low grade and confirm the response before progressing.
subTechniques.reassess: Extension/external rotation and the exact functional restriction.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Anterior glide is not automatically appropriate just because external rotation is limited—use symptom response and stability testing.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid when anterior instability is suspected.
